questions.q: What is the primary goal of writing tests for research code, according to this lesson?
options: Proving the model achieves a target accuracy
Achieving 100% code coverage before any experiment is allowed to run
Replacing the need for a README
Catching silent, expensive bugs — like a reshape or off-by-one label error — before they waste a day of compute
questions.explain: The tests described in this lesson target silent bugs that don't crash but quietly corrupt a run — not proving the model is accurate, which is an experimental result, not a code-correctness question.

questions.q: What does an 'overfit-a-batch' test check, and why is it considered the highest-value test in ML code?
options: That the dataset loader never throws an exception
That training on one fixed batch for many steps drives the loss down sharply, which would fail if gradients weren't flowing or the loss were wired to the wrong tensor
That the model achieves high accuracy on the full validation set
That the model's file size stays under a fixed limit
questions.explain: If a model can't even memorize one fixed batch over many steps, something fundamental is broken in the training wiring — this catches a huge class of bugs that would otherwise only surface as mysteriously slow convergence in a real run.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'assert accuracy > 0.90' is NOT an appropriate unit test?
options: Because accuracy numbers are an experimental result that varies with hardware, data splits, and natural run-to-run variance — not a code-correctness check
Because assert statements are deprecated in modern Python
Because pytest cannot evaluate numeric assertions
Because accuracy should always be exactly 100%
questions.explain: A hard-coded accuracy threshold is a flaky, expensive integration check whose failures often reflect normal variance rather than a bug. Accuracy belongs in experiment tracking, not an assert in a test file.

questions.q: What does a determinism test (same seed, same output) protect against?
options: Uninitialized state, nondeterministic ops, or RNG leaks that would make it impossible to reproduce a previous run's exact result
Using the wrong Python version
Running out of GPU memory
Slow training speed
questions.explain: Reproducible experiment tracking depends on the assumption that re-running with the same seed reproduces the same result. A determinism test catches violations of that assumption before they make a 'reproduce run #214' request impossible.

questions.q: What technique keeps the four recommended tests fast enough to run before every push?
options: Skipping the forward-pass test entirely
Using tiny models and tiny fake batches (e.g. a 2-layer model, batch size of 2) instead of full-scale configs
Running tests only on a separate, unused GPU cluster
Running them only once a month
questions.explain: A small cfg_for_test() with a tiny model and tiny batch catches the same class of bugs as the real config but runs in seconds, keeping the suite fast enough that it actually gets run before every push instead of being skipped.
